story.hook: My coworker kept stealing my lunch.
story.script: For three weeks, food kept disappearing from the office fridge, but only from one shelf: mine. At first I assumed I was forgetting what I had packed. Then an unopened yogurt vanished, followed by half a box of dumplings, and finally a container of curry my mother had made for me the night before. The strange part was that nothing else went missing. My coworkers kept their salads, protein shakes, and sad little sandwiches untouched. Whoever was doing it had apparently decided my lunch was a subscription service. I started writing my name on everything in thick black marker. It did not help. I added a note saying, "Please don't take this. I actually want to eat it." The note disappeared with the food. One afternoon I opened the fridge and found my container back on the shelf, completely empty, with the lid washed and placed neatly on top. That somehow made it worse. Someone had eaten my lunch, cleaned the evidence, and returned the container like they deserved points for manners. I complained in our team chat. Most people reacted with laughing emojis. One coworker, Daniel, said the fridge had become "community property" and joked that I should bring enough for everyone. The next day, I brought enough for exactly one person: me. I packed spicy noodles in a clear container and put my name across the lid. I did not add anything dangerous or strange. I simply ordered them at the level I normally enjoyed, which happened to be much hotter than most people in the office could tolerate. Around noon, I got pulled into a meeting. Ten minutes later, the meeting-room door opened and Daniel rushed past the glass wall toward the pantry. His face was bright red. He grabbed a carton of milk from the shared fridge and drank straight from it. Everyone stared. Our manager asked if he was okay. Daniel coughed, pointed toward the pantry, and said someone had put "insane chili" in the communal noodles. I did not say anything. Then another coworker asked the obvious question: "Which communal noodles?" Daniel froze. The room went completely quiet. He tried to explain that he had thought the container was leftovers from a team lunch. Unfortunately, my name was written across the lid in letters big enough to read from across the pantry. Our manager asked why he had opened food with someone else's name on it. Daniel said he was just checking what it was. Someone at the end of the table laughed and asked whether checking normally required eating half of it. That was when the whole story started coming out. A coworker from finance said she had seen Daniel eating from one of my containers the previous week. Another person remembered him joking that I always brought "restaurant-quality leftovers." Someone else said he had once asked what days my mother usually cooked. Daniel kept insisting it was a misunderstanding, but every new detail somehow made the misunderstanding more specific. Our manager ended the meeting early and asked Daniel to stay behind. I went back to the pantry, opened the fridge, and found my noodles sitting exactly where I had left them, except now there was a fork sticking out of the container and one enormous bite missing. I ate the rest. The next morning, an email went out reminding everyone that personal food was not communal property and that repeated theft from shared spaces could become a conduct issue. Nobody was named. Daniel did not need to be. For the next month, every container in the fridge had a name on it. People started labeling milk, sauces, even a single lemon. Daniel brought his own lunch too. A week later he walked past my desk carrying a plain sandwich and asked, very carefully, whether my food was spicy again. I told him, "Only if you steal it." He laughed like it was a joke. I did not. After that, nothing from my shelf ever disappeared again.
